citations.quote: Based on Industrie 4.0 principles, an overall process for Space Factory 4.0 is proposed. Although the specific case of robotic assembly of modular satellites is focused, this approach is applied to abstract new business models. One of the key features of the overall process is the seamless use of the Digital Twin approach which provides detailed models representing the actual state of a physical component or system. Use-cases such as automated testing and digital product documentation are described to illustrate the benefits of such technology.

Inspired by the opportunities held by manufacturing in space, our objective is to establish new processes and technologies for rapid satellite assembly on an in-orbit platform. This paper introduces methods covering the establishment of new processes based on an Industrie 4.0 approach, the design of highly modular satellites, and their robotic assembly. Additionally, the results obtained through manufacturing prototypes and experiments are discussed to draw conclusions in respect of its benefits and potentials for the space industry.

Reducing redundant testing while guaranteeing quality could be a contribution of the Digital Twin (Section 4), as it stores all available information about the satellites components and allows the execution some of the tests in simulations.

Our Space Factory concept relies on Industrie 4.0 approaches to address the aforementioned challenges in manufacturing in space. As depicted in Fig.1, the concept of a Space Factory 4.0 consists of an in-orbit platform for the fast assembly of modular satellites using robots.

Therefore, we propose an overall process for Space Factory 4.0 by refining a state-of-the art Product Life Cycle (PLC) [9, 10] through the inclusion of Industrie 4.0 concepts. The overall process features three domain-specific processes: Industrie 4.0 Components, Earth Segment, and Space Segment.

The process Industrie 4.0 Components can be regarded as the backbone of the whole process of the Space Factory 4.0 since it continuously integrates specific data from the other processes through semantics and relationships. This is realised by the introduction of the CIB that will be discussed in detail in Section 3. A feature of this process is the extensive use of Digital Twins that are described in Section 4. This process defines formally all necessary steps related to instantiation from reference models, synchronisation using real-time data and administration of Digital Twins.

These processes resemble the concurrent engineering approach [11,12] since they can take place in parallel as long the necessary information for each stage is available upon start. The difference in our approach is that the Industrie 4.0 Components allow a higher adaptability aiming to fulfil the specific requirements of each individualised product.

The main functionalities of a CIB are: 1. Backbone of the overall process Space Factory 4.0 2. Source of information for the definition, representation of reference models, and instantiation of Digital Twins 3. Establishment of interfaces for continuous information exchange between Digital Twins, assembly, support and control systems

A general approach for a CIB comprising the aforementioned functions follows the objectorientated modelling approach [15, 16]. It mainly consists of a core model called Centralised Information Base and partial models such as Software System, Product, Support systems & Operations, Space Segment and Production.

The Satellite is the physical entity of a CubeSat with a construction (mechanical, electrical, sensors etc.), functions, location (also regarding traceability along the product life cycle), and performance. An entity of a Satellite is configurable and built up by modules that are predefined in a repository or library. Furthermore, specific boundary conditions of the modules and its components such as the necessary tolerances or insertion forces of the 50pin headers included as properties.
The Satellite is bidirectionally associated with its Digital Twin instance, which digitally represents its actual state using real time data with models (this is explained in Section 4).

Each Software Module can be directly associated with a Satellite Module within the partial model Product. This interface enables the most important approaches of this project - namely, the main software of the satellite is assembled according to the modular configuration of a specific CubeSat.
It provides a reference architecture and provides the foundation of Digital Twin approach as well as its related support systems.

One of the key approaches of Industrie 4.0 - the Digital Twin is the digital representation of the physical product or process characterised by a seamless communication based on real-time data. The concept of the Digital Twin is particularly useful for assets with CPS, since the physical component of the CPS and its interaction with the digital component can be accurately represented and simulated. The Digital Twin represents the current state of a product or process through all phases of a PLC.

For the Space Factory 4.0, the asset of the Digital Twin comprises further subcomponents such as the digital representation of the physical product (e.g. CubeSats as described in Section 5) as well as simulation models (e.g. Finite-Element-Analysis (FEA) and Multi-Body-Simulation (MBS)). The simulations models are directly coupled to the product and its related processes aiming to reproduce the interactions with the environment using real time data.

Therefore, the definition of a Space Factory 4.0 Component (SF4.0-Component) is introduced aiming to extend the functionalities of an I4.0 component by the capability of interpreting TM/TC that are now defined in the CIB.

Three modules for assembling the CubeSat are considered: backplane, Attitude Determination and Control System (ADCS), and On-Board Data Handling (OBDH). - Focus on the mechanical and geometrical properties of the hardware and software of each module. Electronics are assumed to be black boxes.

Asset: 3D CAD models for the product representation of the CubeSat modules backplane, ADCS, OBDH, and power. We use Siemens NX as a 3D CAD system. - Manifest: Mainly derived from the CIB, a modular data exchange format is populated. - Component manager: The component manager is a further development of the software system developed in [22]. It comprises of a Java program and a web app.

At last, the CIB provides the SF4.0 app the fundamental structure to instantiate Digital Twins by assembling models of the hardware and its related software modules. For that, a unique ID is assigned to each Digital Twin instance and directly associated to a unique IP address. Additionally, the SF4.0 app provides a graphical user interface (GUI) for data as well as parameters input, and configuration control of the Digital Twin.

To test our implementation, we follow some steps of the overall process Space Factory 4.0 (see Fig. 2) that are listed below: 1. Product planning step at earth segment: A costumer accesses the SF 4.0 app using a webbrowser and configures an individualised CubeSat 2. Initiation of SF4.0 components such as CIB and reference models: During the configuration, the 3D CAD model of the CubeSat is automatically generated along with their corresponding software modules 3. Instantiation of Digital Twin: as a SF4.0 component is instantiated including unique ID 4. Interface between Digital Twin Instance, Production and Testing: Update and synchronisation of the Digital Twin instance using feedback data from the assembly process.

The tests revealed that a Digital Twin is successfully generated in an automated way based on the inputs of the costumer (as shown in Fig. 5). Each configuration is assigned to a unique ID which can be accessed through the internet (e.g. web browser).

The functional tests inspect whether modules are working or not by powering them during their integration. For this paper, we defined Booleans (True for working or False for not working) as a data type. After the functional test is conducted, an event query is triggered and sent in real-time from the assembly process to the Digital Twin.

In particular, the capabilities of the Digital Twin to update CAD models and simulation models based on real-time data gathered with high frequency (>1 kHz) from the assembly and operation processes are not in the scope of this paper and will be explored in future works. Additionally, the TM/TC interpreter component of the administration shell of SF4.0-components still have to be implemented in the context of executing automated tests with Digital Twins and will be scope of future publications.

The UNISEC CubeSat Interface Definition (CSID) [29] promoted by UNISEC Europe was first implemented in UWE-3, the third generation of the University of Wurzburg satellites. Launched back in 2013 and being still operational now after 5 years, this satellite bus presents clearly a robust alternative to PC/104.

The European members of UNISEC agreed on using the CSID in their CubeSat projects and other UNISEC members already implemented the CSID e.g. the 8 satellites in the BIRDS-1 and BIRDS-2 CubeSat constellations.

The CSID is based on a modular system design approach with modular subsystems connected to a backplane which offers scalability and redundancy. For example, if a satellite requires more power, it is possible to connect further electronic power systems (EPS) to the bus, without any adaptions required to the rest of the satellite. This enables the individualisation of satellites based on the customer needs.

The 50-pin headers require only around 9N insertion force and allow a misalignment tolerance of 0.7mm. The standard includes all required signals for operation, testing and debugging on the satellite bus with dedicated signal lines for most crucial subsystems and therefore requires no extra harnessing. The backplane based design offers access to inserted subsystems individually and provides the ability to test these subsystems already during integration.

Several testing steps are also demonstrated. Automated general functional tests of the subsystems are performed before and during the mounting to the backplane. They show if a subsystem works as expected, both before and after integration. When the satellite is fully integrated, an automated functional test including sensor stimulation and calibration will be demonstrated using high precision motion simulators at Zentrum fur Telematik e.V.

After the customer decides on a specific satellite configuration that was instantiated as a Digital Twin as described in Section 4.2, the integration environment is commanded to start with the automated integration of the subsystems according to this configuration. The robot picks the first subsystem (A in Fig. 10) in the tray and moves it to the visual inspection unit. Here, the subsystem is visually analysed in order to identify the subsystem and check if human interaction is required. Then, the robot places the subsystem in a test environment, where software unit tests are performed. If these tests are successful, the subsystem is mounted to the backplane B, followed again by software unit tests. These tests ensure that the subsystem was mounted to the backplane correctly. If successful, the next subsystem is picked. Throughout all these integration and verification steps, the Digital Twin instance is constantly updated with the corresponding measurements and can command intervention from the robot in case it identifies an error in the assembly.
The representation of the whole satellite as Digital Twin as discussed in Section 4 is a huge advantage compared to the current paperbased approach in space technology. Monitoring,

The robot offers 7 degrees of freedom per arm and an end-effector accuracy of 0.1mm. It provides force-sensitive gripping functionality and a maximum payload capability of 0.5kg. With these specifications, the robot meets the requirements for the automated integration demonstration task.

Special attention has been directed to the gripper design. Since the UNISEC CSID is initially not developed to offer automation capabilities, there is no specific area on the surface of the subsystem PCBs where gripping is allowed. Also gripping at the edges of the subsystem is not reliable, since there is no restriction of placing parts close to the edges. However, there exist four mounting holes to connect the PCB to the structure, after the subsystems are mounted to the backplane. These holes are surrounded by a specific area, where no parts are allowed to be placed. Therefore, we developed a gripper to grip the subsystem via two of these holes, which results in precise handling of the subsystems. With this gripper, the ABB Yumi robot is able to perform the automated integration of several subsystems.

The motion simulator performs specific motion manoeuvres to stimulate the sensors, while the sensor output is written to the Digital Twin. The Digital Twin calculates the calibration matrix of each sensor and immediately notices misalignments or problems with functionality of the sensor.

In a pilot test, the usability of the virtual fixtures was investigated. To this end, a placing experiment was conducted five times for one subject with and without the support of virtual fixtures respectively. The goal was to reach a plugging position at the required accuracy just above the electric plugs. The results show the mean time without virtual fixtures was 8.0s (standard deviation 1.2s) and with virtual fixtures was 4.6s (standard deviation 0.5s). The virtual fixtures appear to improve time to reach the target position by over 40%. Further tests could reveal whether this effect is significant and what types of virtual fixtures are helpful.
We demonstrated, on an Earth Factory, the technologies necessary to automate the integration and testing of CubeSat modules, which can be transferred onto an in-orbit platform.

The proposed concept for a CIB provides a reference architecture and represents the foundation of the Digital Twin approach as well as its related support systems. In practice, it is a platform providing individual tools and information for every step of the overall process Space Factory 4.0. The approach of the CIB is very promising. However, due to its complexity, a full implementation of the CIB is outside the scope of our conceptual study.

One challenge of implementing Digital Twins is their complexity in respect of the level of detail necessary to achieve these objectives. Future work should extend our concept to consider, for example, the electrical part of the Digital Twin.

Automation of the satellite integration and testing significantly shortens production cycles, reduces cost and simultaneously improves quality. Furthermore, automation enables the production of satellites in hazardous environments.

Satellites that implement the UNISEC Europe CSID enable the automation of the integration process as demonstrated in this paper. However further research is required for a full integration of a CubeSat based on this design.

One challenge that has been addressed but is yet to be tested is time delay - communication with space results in a considerable latency. The framework in [33] can account for this, but further tests are necessary to see how control can be shared between the virtual environment (i.e. virtual fixtures) and the force-feedback from the real environment. Depending on the available communication bandwidth and the complexity of the task, more or less autonomy may be required on the slave side.
